newsitem.title: EGYPT: FEATURE-Egyptian women suffer violence in silence.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Egyptian women suffer violence in silence.

text.p: Marlene Tadros, a veteran Egyptian human rights activist, was so enraged to hear a male activist tell a visiting U.S. official there was no wife beating in Egypt that she set out to prove him wrong.
She began interviewing women in Cairo in January and now jokes she might as well fill in the rest of the questionnaires herself because her findings were depressingly uniform.
Each of the nearly 200 women she talked to has been beaten.
A larger survey showed a lower rate -- about one woman in three since marriage -- but it confirmed Tadros's findings that most women thought husbands sometimes had a right to beat them.

"Very few of the women stood up to the men. They're taught this is the natural thing. Some even said this is what marriage is about," said Tadros, executive director of the Legal Research and Resource Centre for Human Rights.

A 30-year-old woman said her husband was first violent on their wedding night and continues to beat her with his hands, a stick and cables. He throws cups and plates at her, kicks her, pulls her hair and swears at her, the woman said.
The reason for his violence is mainly to obtain sex but she said her security guard husband also beats her if she asks for more household expenses and that he beats their daughters too.

"On my wedding night he was a stranger. I pushed him away from me so he beat me up. Now, he beats me up and sleeps with me and says it is not up to you. He is stupid and merciless. He is heartless. He is not a human being," the woman said.
The women who spoke to Tadros live in a low-income area and are mostly illiterate.
SIX SCENARIOS FOR JUSTIFIED BEATINGS
The larger survey, published by the government's National Population Council (NPC), says that domestic abuse cut across educational and income levels.
It also said that 86 percent of woman interviewed for the study agreed that husbands are justified in beating their wives under at least one of six scenarios presented to them.
Women were most likely to agree that men are justified in beating their wives if she refuses sex or answers him back.
The other scenarios in descending order of acceptability were if the wife talks to other men, if she neglects the children, if the wife wastes money and if she burns food.

Of the one-in-three women beaten at least once since marriage, 45 percent had been beaten at least once in the year prior to the survey and 17 percent had been beaten three or more times in the same period, it found.
Pregnancy does not protect women from violence, the survey found. About one third of the women who reported being beaten were abused during pregnancy.

Official figures on domestic abuse are rare in Egypt. Activists say the study, for which researchers interviewed 7,121 women aged 15 to 49 who were or had been married, is believed to be the largest on the topic.

Reuters tried in vain to obtain a copy from the NPC and eventually received one from an unofficial source. The government was embarrassed by the findings and was trying to keep them from reaching the media, activists said.
Women's activists blame rigid religious and cultural teachings that dictate gender rights and expectations and lax legislation for the prevalence of wife beating.
DIVORCE IS POSSIBLE BUT DIFFICULT

"There has to be awareness through media campaigns. There are women being at least slapped in all our films and television shows and these women then fall for the man. There is a concept that women want this sadistic, macho man. The shows have a lot to do with making it acceptable," Tadros told Reuters.
An unusual case Tadros came across involved a 45-year-old woman who lives with her ex-husband and his new wife because she has nowhere else to go and does not want to leave her children.
The woman complained her ex-husband beat her into having sex with him and that he was violent if she spent a lot of money.
A woman in Egypt can file for divorce if she is beaten but few do so because of difficulties such as unresponsive police and the need to provide witnesses for the case to stand up.
If a woman makes it to court, rights activists complain that judges often base their verdict on her social class, with the assumption that poor women are used to such violence.

"It is humiliation every step of the way. Proof of injury means a lot of these women who live in dire economic circumstances just live with violence and accept it," said Dr Magda Adli, a physician at the Nadim Centre for the Management and Rehabilitation of Victims of Violence.
One of the centre's success stories was a 21-year-old woman whose husband beat and humiliated her to such an extent over a two-year period that she lost the ability to read and write.
Therapy helped the woman, who holds a trade diploma, regain confidence in herself and stand up to her husband, Adli said.
